source.title: Choosing the right basis for interpretability: Psychophysical comparison between neuron-based and dictionary-based representations
source.authors: Julien Colin; L. Goetschalckx; Thomas Fel; Victor Boutin; Thomas Serre; Nuria Oliver

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on superposition-related representation geometry and interpretability in pretrained vision CNNs, extending the discussion to a new model setting with different measurements. It does not test the specified toy-model or LLM claims.
record.gate_note: The paper measures dictionary-element axis-alignment as a proxy for superposition and compares human judgments of neuron- and dictionary-based representations. The decision-importance comparison is a fairness check, not a test of whether feature importance determines dimension allocation. Cited findings from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study assumes superposition to motivate NMF dictionaries in two ImageNet vision CNNs, then reports human visual-coherence scores for dictionary versus neuron units. Its one superposition-related measure is Hoyer axis-alignment of dictionary elements, which the authors call a proxy. No version matches this setting. V1 needs toy models, and V4 names LLMs. V5 needs completeness, stability or canonicity, none of which is assessed. No version is tested, so no verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors find the models rely no less on dictionary elements than on neurons for their decisions. Also add that ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 only under the dictionary basis, contradicting the neuron-based Zimmermann et al. comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CRAFT, based on non-negative matrix factorization, to obtain dictionary elements from CNN activations and evaluates visual coherence through human psychophysics. It does not reproduce the original toy-model intervention or measure its sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes varied with representational basis, model, and layer depth. Dictionary-based interpretability increased significantly with relative depth in both models; the neuron-based depth correlations were weaker and not significant after correction.

fits_no_version.finding: Humans picked the correct query more often for NMF dictionary units than neuron units: 83.5 vs 78.8 (Exp I), 85.1 vs 76.2 (Exp II), 81.5 vs 77.1 (Exp III, VGG16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision CNNs, dictionary-learned directions are more visually coherent to humans than neuron axes.

fits_no_version.finding: Dictionary-unit interpretability correlated with layer depth (r=0.35 and r=0.38). Neuron-unit correlations were not significant after Bonferroni correction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision CNNs, the dictionary-basis interpretability advantage grows with layer depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean Hoyer axis-alignment of CRAFT elements was lower in ResNet50 than in VGG16 (0.40 vs 0.45, p<.001). The authors read this as more superposition in ResNet50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision CNNs differ in how distributed their dictionary features are across neurons. This would extend V4's indirect-evidence claim to non-LLM models.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to two pretrained vision CNNs and a human visual-coherence task. The authors say semantic confounding was only partially addressed in Experiment II. Dictionary elements were learned from the top 300 activating images for each selected neuron, and one element was selected for comparison; the authors note that future work should apply dictionary learning to full-layer activations.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result meeting the row criteria was omitted. The decision-importance comparisons in Section 4.1 were excluded because they assess matched decision relevance, not the claim's feature-capacity or geometry propositions.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature-to-dimension sweep, no sparsity transition and no geometry.
Capacity competition and importance-based dimension allocation are not tested. The Sec 4.1 importance check only matches decision relevance.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not examined.
No LLMs are studied. The analogous vision-CNN result (dictionary elements spread across neurons, ResNet50 more than VGG16) falls outside the version's named system.
Completeness, stability and canonicity are not assessed. One NMF element per neuron is judged only for human coherence.
There is no comparison of one-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Cross-model tests. Dictionary basis: ResNet50 85.1 vs VGG16 81.5 (z=2.14, p=0.016). Neuron basis: no difference (z=0.56, p=0.71).
Decision-importance check (Gradient×Input). No difference in ResNet50 (p=0.36). Dictionary elements slightly more important in VGG16 (p=0.001).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' conflicts with its own finding that no version is tested; it is changed to uses_without_test. The superposition claim here is interpretive. The dictionaries (k=10, learned on each neuron's top 300 images, most-frequent element chosen) are a weak probe of superposition, and the authors themselves say full-layer dictionaries are needed. If V4 were broadened beyond LLMs, r11/r12 would be a weak, proxy-based partial support.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, controlled feature-to-dimension ratios, sparsity sweep, transition, or regular feature geometry are tested.
The study does not test capacity competition or whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemantic neurons are evidence for superposition.
The models are vision CNNs, not LLMs; no LLM feature distribution or SAE recovery is tested.
The study does not establish dictionary features as complete, stable, or canonical units. It uses NMF/CRAFT, not SAEs, and evaluates human visual coherence.
Dictionary elements are directions in the method, but the study does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Measured average axis-alignment of CRAFT dictionary elements using Hoyer sparsity.
rows.measure: Average dictionary-element axis-alignment score (lower values indicate elements more distributed across neurons)
rows.note: The authors interpret the lower score as indicating greater distribution across neurons and suggest greater superposition.
rows.check: This is a proxy measure in vision CNNs, not LLMs. Dictionaries were learned per neuron over its top 300 images, not over full-layer activations. r11 and r12 record the same single comparison.

rows.subject: VGG16
rows.operation_detail: Measured average axis-alignment of CRAFT dictionary elements using Hoyer sparsity.
rows.measure: Average dictionary-element axis-alignment score (higher values indicate elements more aligned with individual neuron axes)
rows.note: The authors interpret the higher score as indicating dictionary elements more aligned with individual neuron axes.
rows.check: Comparator duplicate of r11, reporting the same Mann–Whitney test.
